tip: Own body parts take 'the', not 'her', in French: s'est coupé les ongles = cut her nails. The reflexive se already tells you whose nails they are, so les does the rest.
Depuis wants the present, not the past: elle le connaît depuis longtemps = she has known him a long time. Started back then and still true? French stays in present tense.
The -s on appelés is doing grammar: when a direct object (les) sits before avoir, the participle agrees with it. Les = them (masc.), so appelé gains an s.
After a preposition, te turns into toi: c'est pour toi, never 'pour te'. Once a word like pour or avec comes first, French switches to the stressed pronoun.
Two pronouns stack in a fixed order before the verb: leur en, never 'en leur'. Here leur = to them and en = about it: je leur en ai parlé.
S'entendre literally means 'hear each other', but nous nous entendons très bien = we get along great. In French, getting on well is a matter of hearing each other well.
To agree is 'put yourselves in agreement': se mettre d'accord. Elles se sont mises d'accord = they came to an agreement, literally placed themselves in accord.
